claim: Rad52 is the functional homolog of BRCA2 in yeast.
source: Rad52, the functional homolog of BRCA2 in yeast, accumulates at DSB sites and diffuses ~6 times faster within repair foci than the focus itself, exhibiting confined motion.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Rad52 accumulates at DSB sites.
source: Rad52, the functional homolog of BRCA2 in yeast, accumulates at DSB sites and diffuses ~6 times faster within repair foci than the focus itself, exhibiting confined motion.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Rad52 diffuses approximately 6 times faster within repair foci than the focus itself.
source: Rad52, the functional homolog of BRCA2 in yeast, accumulates at DSB sites and diffuses ~6 times faster within repair foci than the focus itself, exhibiting confined motion.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Rad52 exhibits confined motion within repair foci.
source: Rad52, the functional homolog of BRCA2 in yeast, accumulates at DSB sites and diffuses ~6 times faster within repair foci than the focus itself, exhibiting confined motion.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and demonstrated through MSD analysis in the results.

claim: The Rad52 confinement radius coincides with the focus size.
source: The Rad52 confinement radius coincides with the focus size: foci resulting from 2 DSBs are twice larger in volume that the ones induced by a unique DSB and the Rad52 confinement radius scales accordingly.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental measurements comparing single and double DSB conditions.

claim: Foci resulting from 2 DSBs are twice larger in volume than the ones induced by a unique DSB.
source: The Rad52 confinement radius coincides with the focus size: foci resulting from 2 DSBs are twice larger in volume that the ones induced by a unique DSB and the Rad52 confinement radius scales accordingly.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the abstract and supported by PALM data in the results.

claim: The Rad52 confinement radius scales with focus size when comparing 1 DSB to 2 DSBs.
source: The Rad52 confinement radius coincides with the focus size: foci resulting from 2 DSBs are twice larger in volume that the ones induced by a unique DSB and the Rad52 confinement radius scales accordingly.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by comparing confinement radii under different DSB conditions.

claim: Rfa1 molecules follow anomalous diffusion similar to the focus itself or damaged chromatin.
source: In contrast, molecules of the single strand binding protein Rfa1 follow anomalous diffusion similar to the focus itself or damaged chromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by MSD analysis showing anomalous exponents.

claim: Most Rfa1 molecules are bound to ssDNA.
source: We conclude that while most Rfa1 molecules are bound to the ssDNA, Rad52 molecules are free to explore the entire focus reflecting the existence of a liquid droplet around damaged DNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the diffusion behavior of Rfa1 compared to Rad52.

claim: Rad52 molecules are free to explore the entire focus.
source: We conclude that while most Rfa1 molecules are bound to the ssDNA, Rad52 molecules are free to explore the entire focus reflecting the existence of a liquid droplet around damaged DNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the confined diffusion behavior and confinement radius measurements.

claim: Repair foci reflect the existence of a liquid droplet around damaged DNA.
source: We conclude that while most Rfa1 molecules are bound to the ssDNA, Rad52 molecules are free to explore the entire focus reflecting the existence of a liquid droplet around damaged DNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including mobility, confinement, and hexanediol sensitivity.

claim: Repair proteins accumulate at damaged sites forming membrane-less sub-compartments or foci in response to double strand breaks.
source: In response to double strand breaks (DSB), repair proteins accumulate at damaged sites, forming membrane-less sub-compartments or foci.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is established knowledge supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: DSBs are the most genotoxic kind of DNA damage.
source: Among the different kinds of DNA damages, DSBs are the most genotoxic (Iliakis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Failure to repair DSBs leads to genomic instability or cell death.
source: Failure to repair such lesions leads to genomic instability or cell death, and mutations in DNA repair genes lead to diseases such as Werner, Bloom and other cancer predisposition syndromes (Rassool, 2003; Thorslund and West, 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Mutations in DNA repair genes lead to diseases such as Werner, Bloom and other cancer predisposition syndromes.
source: Failure to repair such lesions leads to genomic instability or cell death, and mutations in DNA repair genes lead to diseases such as Werner, Bloom and other cancer predisposition syndromes (Rassool, 2003; Thorslund and West, 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Eukaryotic organisms use mainly two major mechanisms to repair DSBs: non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination (HR).
source: Eukaryotic organisms use mainly two major mechanisms to repair DSBs: non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination (HR) (Wyman and Kanaar, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: HR occurs primarily in S/G2 phase cells.
source: HR occurs primarily in S/G2 phase cells and uses an undamaged homologous DNA sequence as a template for copying the missing information (Lisby and Rothstein, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: HR uses an undamaged homologous DNA sequence as a template for copying the missing information.
source: HR occurs primarily in S/G2 phase cells and uses an undamaged homologous DNA sequence as a template for copying the missing information (Lisby and Rothstein, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: HR is orchestrated by mega-Dalton multi-protein complexes of 500 to 2000 proteins that colocalize with the DSB.
source: HR is orchestrated by mega-Dalton multi-protein complexes of 500 to 2000 proteins that colocalize with the DSB (Lisby et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated with a citation providing quantitative information about repair complexes.

claim: Rad52 protein stimulates the removal of RPA and recruits the recombinase Rad51 to the ssDNA tail.
source: The Rad52 protein, the functional analog of human BRCA2 in yeast, then stimulates the removal of RPA and recruits the recombinase Rad51 to the ssDNA tail on which it polymerizes (Symington et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and represents established knowledge about Rad52 function.

claim: The Rad51-ssDNA complex is called a nucleo-filament.
source: The Rad51-ssDNA complex, called a nucleo-filament, has the capacity to search and identify a region of homology and to promote strand invasion of the homologous duplex DNA (Bordelet and Dubrana, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and represents established terminology.

claim: The Rad51-ssDNA nucleo-filament has the capacity to search and identify a region of homology and to promote strand invasion of the homologous duplex DNA.
source: The Rad51-ssDNA complex, called a nucleo-filament, has the capacity to search and identify a region of homology and to promote strand invasion of the homologous duplex DNA (Bordelet and Dubrana, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and represents established knowledge about Rad51 function.

claim: Recent works proposed that repair proteins exhibit some properties of liquid-like droplets such as Rad52 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast.
source: In particular, recent works proposed that repair proteins exhibit some properties of liquid-like droplets such as Rad52 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast (Oshidari et al., 2020) and 53BP1 in human cells (Altmeyer et al., 2015; Kilic et al., 2019; Pessina et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations to recent literature.

claim: Recent works proposed that 53BP1 in human cells exhibits some properties of liquid-like droplets.
source: In particular, recent works proposed that repair proteins exhibit some properties of liquid-like droplets such as Rad52 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast (Oshidari et al., 2020) and 53BP1 in human cells (Altmeyer et al., 2015; Kilic et al., 2019; Pessina et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations to recent literature.

claim: Rad52 exhibits two diffusive behaviors in the absence of DSB with diffusion coefficients D1 = 1.16 ± 0.08 μm2/s and D2 = 0.28 ± 0.02 μm2/s.
source: We obtained D1/S-G2 = 1.16 ± 0.08 μm2/s, D2/S-G2 = 0.28 ± 0.02 μm2/s as the best-fit diffusion coefficients (see Materials and methods), with the fraction of slow molecules being 0.62 ± 0.04.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from displacement histogram analysis.

claim: The fraction of slow Rad52 molecules in the absence of DSB is 0.62 ± 0.04.
source: We obtained D1/S-G2 = 1.16 ± 0.08 μm2/s, D2/S-G2 = 0.28 ± 0.02 μm2/s as the best-fit diffusion coefficients (see Materials and methods), with the fraction of slow molecules being 0.62 ± 0.04.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from displacement histogram analysis.

claim: The average trajectory length of Rad52 in the absence of DSB is 7.5 frames.
source: After examining 23 cells in S/G2 phase of the cell cycle as assessed by the presence and the size of a bud on the transmission image, we obtained an exponentially decreasing distribution of trace lengths with an average trajectory length of 7.5 frames, the longest trace reaching 65 frames (1.3 s) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from tracking data.

claim: The longest Rad52 trace in the absence of DSB reaches 65 frames (1.3 s).
source: After examining 23 cells in S/G2 phase of the cell cycle as assessed by the presence and the size of a bud on the transmission image, we obtained an exponentially decreasing distribution of trace lengths with an average trajectory length of 7.5 frames, the longest trace reaching 65 frames (1.3 s) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from tracking data.

claim: The half-life time of JF646 is 2.1 s.
source: Since the half-life time of JF646 is 2.1 s (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), the short trace lengths observed here are due to molecules moving out of the observable z-section and not the photo bleaching of the JF646 dyes.
evidence: This is a measurement stated in the text and shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: The short trace lengths of Rad52 in the absence of DSB are due to molecules moving out of the observable z-section and not the photo bleaching of the JF646 dyes.
source: Since the half-life time of JF646 is 2.1 s (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), the short trace lengths observed here are due to molecules moving out of the observable z-section and not the photo bleaching of the JF646 dyes.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the bleaching time to the trace lengths.

claim: Rad52 diffusion does not change significantly during the cell cycle.
source: Thus, Rad52 diffusion does not change significantly during the cell cycle and the two observed Rad52 populations cannot be simply explained by free versus Rad52 molecules transiently associated with the replication fork.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing G1 and S/G2 phase measurements.

claim: The two observed Rad52 populations cannot be simply explained by free versus Rad52 molecules transiently associated with the replication fork.
source: Thus, Rad52 diffusion does not change significantly during the cell cycle and the two observed Rad52 populations cannot be simply explained by free versus Rad52 molecules transiently associated with the replication fork.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the similarity of diffusion in G1 and S/G2 phases.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of free Halo-NLS is 1.90 ± 0.06 μm2/s.
source: We found a diffusion coefficient of DfreeHalo-NLS = 1.90 ± 0.06 μm2/s, consistent with previous studies by FRAP (Larson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a measurement stated in the text with a citation for comparison.

claim: The dynamic viscosity in the yeast nucleus is 0.122 ± 0.004 Pa.s.
source: From this measurement, we extracted a dynamic viscosity in the yeast nucleus of 0.122 ± 0.004 Pa.s.
evidence: This is calculated from the free Halo-NLS diffusion measurement using the Stokes-Einstein equation.

claim: The predicted diffusion coefficients of Rad52 monomers and multimers are Dmonomer = 1.20 ± 0.04 μm2/s and Dmultimer = 0.28 ± 0.01 μm2/s.
source: Using this measured viscosity, the predicted diffusion coefficients of Rad52 monomers and multimers are Dmonomer = 1.20 ± 0.04 μm2/s and Dmultimer = 0.28 ± 0.01 μm2/s (see Materials and methods), consistent with the two populations D1 = 1.16 ± 0.08 and D2 = 0.28 ± 0.02 obtained experimentally.
evidence: This is calculated using the Stokes-Einstein equation and measured viscosity.

claim: The measured diffusion coefficients of Rad52 are consistent with the existence of a mixed population of Rad52 inside nuclei, approximately 2/3 being multimers.
source: Thus, our measurements of Rad52 diffusion by SPT are consistent with the existence of a mixed population of Rad52 inside nuclei,~2/3 being multimers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing predicted and measured diffusion coefficients.

claim: Inside foci, Rad52 exhibits a diffusion coefficient of DRad52,inside = 0.032 ± 0.006 μm2/s.
source: This analysis revealed that Rad52 molecules inside foci exhibit a confined motion with a confinement radius Rc = 124 ± 3 nm and a diffusion coefficient DRad52,inside = 0.032 ± 0.006 μm2/s (see Methods and Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a measurement from MSD analysis.

claim: Inside foci, Rad52 exhibits a confinement radius of Rc = 124 ± 3 nm.
source: This analysis revealed that Rad52 molecules inside foci exhibit a confined motion with a confinement radius Rc = 124 ± 3 nm and a diffusion coefficient DRad52,inside = 0.032 ± 0.006 μm2/s (see Methods and Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a measurement from MSD analysis.

claim: SUMOylated Rad52 exhibits a diffusion coefficient inside foci of DRad52-SUMO, inside = 0.009 ± 0.002 μm2/s.
source: Inside foci, SUMOylated Rad52 also exhibits confined diffusion although with slower diffusion coefficient (DRad52-Sumo, inside = 0.009 ± 0.002 μm2/s, Figure 2J and Supplementary file 1) and a smaller confinement radius than wild type Rad52 (Rc Rad52-SUMO = 83 ± 12 nm versus Rc Rad52 = 124 ± 3 nm).
evidence: This is a measurement from MSD analysis comparing SUMOylated and wild type Rad52.

claim: SUMOylated Rad52 has a smaller confinement radius than wild type Rad52 (Rc Rad52-SUMO = 83 ± 12 nm versus Rc Rad52 = 124 ± 3 nm).
source: Inside foci, SUMOylated Rad52 also exhibits confined diffusion although with slower diffusion coefficient (DRad52-Sumo, inside = 0.009 ± 0.002 μm2/s, Figure 2J and Supplementary file 1) and a smaller confinement radius than wild type Rad52 (Rc Rad52-SUMO = 83 ± 12 nm versus Rc Rad52 = 124 ± 3 nm).
evidence: This is a measurement from MSD analysis comparing SUMOylated and wild type Rad52.

claim: SUMOylated Rad52 foci are smaller and denser than wild type foci.
source: We propose that when all Rad52 molecules are SUMOylated, Rad52 foci transition to a gel-like sub-compartment where most of the molecules are still free to explore the whole focus but much slower than in wild type cells. Since SUMOylated Rad52 foci are smaller, it is possible that the formation of LLPS around damage sites is a mechanism to increase the pull of molecules at the DSB.
evidence: This is stated based on measurements of focus size and intensity.

claim: Individual Rad52 molecules diffuse 6.4 times faster than the whole focus.
source: Using both displacement histograms and MSD analysis (Figure 3C–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we found that Rad52 molecules diffuse 6.4 times faster than the whole focus (DRad52 inside = 0.032 ± 0.006 μm2/s versus Dwhole focus = 0.005 ± 0.002 μm2/s, assuming normal diffusion with a time difference of 20 ms for the whole focus).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison based on measured diffusion coefficients.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of the whole Rad52 focus is Dwhole focus = 0.005 ± 0.002 μm2/s.
source: Using both displacement histograms and MSD analysis (Figure 3C–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we found that Rad52 molecules diffuse 6.4 times faster than the whole focus (DRad52 inside = 0.032 ± 0.006 μm2/s versus Dwhole focus = 0.005 ± 0.002 μm2/s, assuming normal diffusion with a time difference of 20 ms for the whole focus).
evidence: This is a measurement from tracking the entire focus.

claim: The MSD of the whole Rad52 focus fits better with an anomalous diffusion of anomalous exponent 0.51 ± 0.05.
source: Furthermore, the shape of the MSD fits better with an anomalous diffusion of anomalous exponent 0.51 ± 0.05, as previously reported for damaged chromatin at that time scale (Miné-Hattab et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a measurement from MSD analysis with a citation for comparison.

claim: Individual Rfa1 molecules are less mobile than individual Rad52 molecules inside foci.
source: Comparing the displacement histograms of individual Rfa1 and Rad52 molecules, we found that Rfa1 is less mobile than individual Rad52 molecules inside foci (Figure 4C) and exhibits a mobility similar to whole Rad52 foci (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on comparing displacement histograms.

claim: Rfa1 exhibits a mobility similar to whole Rad52 foci.
source: Comparing the displacement histograms of individual Rfa1 and Rad52 molecules, we found that Rfa1 is less mobile than individual Rad52 molecules inside foci (Figure 4C) and exhibits a mobility similar to whole Rad52 foci (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on comparing displacement histograms.

claim: Rfa1 exhibits an apparent normal diffusion coefficient DRfa1 = 0.006 ± 0.001 μm2/s inside foci.
source: Using both Rfa1 displacement histograms and MSD analysis inside foci, Rfa1 exhibits an apparent normal diffusion coefficient DRfa1 = 0.006 ± 0.001 μm2/s (Figure 4E, assuming normal diffusion with a time difference of 20 ms).
evidence: This is a measurement from displacement histogram and MSD analysis.

claim: The MSD of Rfa1 inside foci has an anomalous exponent of 0.56 ± 0.05.
source: Moreover, the MSD of Rfa1 inside foci is similar to the entire focus, with an anomalous exponent of 0.56 ± 0.05 (Figure 4E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a measurement from MSD analysis.

claim: The percentage of S-phase cells containing a Rad52 focus significantly decreases after 1.6-hexanediol treatment (from 22 ± 2% to 8 ± 3%).
source: We found that the percentage of S-phase cells containing a Rad52 focus significantly decreases after 1.6-hexanediol treatment (22 ± 2% to 8 ± 3% respectively), consistent with recent work (Oshidari et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from imaging cells under different treatment conditions.

claim: The percentage of Rfa1 foci remains similar with or without hexanediol treatment.
source: In contrast, the percentage of Rfa1 foci remains similar with or without hexanediol treatment (Figure 4G, left and middle panels).
evidence: This is based on quantifying foci under different treatment conditions.

claim: Rad52 foci are not visible after fixation with several classical fixation methods.
source: We also noticed that after fixation with several classical fixation methods (Methods), Rad52 foci are not visible and Edc3 foci are significantly less abundant (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 respectively), while Rfa1 foci are not altered by fixation (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is an observation from imaging fixed cells.

claim: Rfa1 foci are not altered by fixation.
source: We also noticed that after fixation with several classical fixation methods (Methods), Rad52 foci are not visible and Edc3 foci are significantly less abundant (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 respectively), while Rfa1 foci are not altered by fixation (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is an observation from imaging fixed cells.

claim: The mean residence time of Rad52 inside foci is approximately 240 ms.
source: We found that the mean residence time of Rad52 inside foci, defined as the integral of the survival probability curve, is ~240 ms while Rfa1 molecules stay longer (560 ms) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is calculated from the survival probability curve.

claim: The mean residence time of Rfa1 inside foci is approximately 560 ms.
source: We found that the mean residence time of Rad52 inside foci, defined as the integral of the survival probability curve, is ~240 ms while Rfa1 molecules stay longer (560 ms) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is calculated from the survival probability curve.

claim: 70% of Rad52 traces cross a focus boundary at least once during the 20 s movie.
source: Among the first 2 categories of traces, 70% cross a focus boundary at least once during the 20 s movie, while 30% stay inside foci, indicating that Rad52 foci are in constant exchange with the rest of the nucleus.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from analyzing trace categories.

claim: 30% of Rad52 traces stay inside foci during the 20 s movie.
source: Among the first 2 categories of traces, 70% cross a focus boundary at least once during the 20 s movie, while 30% stay inside foci, indicating that Rad52 foci are in constant exchange with the rest of the nucleus.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from analyzing trace categories.

claim: Rad52 foci are in constant exchange with the rest of the nucleus.
source: Among the first 2 categories of traces, 70% cross a focus boundary at least once during the 20 s movie, while 30% stay inside foci, indicating that Rad52 foci are in constant exchange with the rest of the nucleus.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the high percentage of traces crossing boundaries.

claim: Only 33% of Rfa1 molecules cross a focus boundary.
source: As a comparison, only 33% of Rfa1 molecules cross a focus boundary.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement for comparison with Rad52.

claim: Rad52 molecules change diffusion coefficient when entering or escaping repair foci.
source: In other words, Rad52 molecules clearly change diffusion coefficient when entering or escaping repair foci, adopting the diffusive behavior of the surrounding Rad52 molecules in their environment.
evidence: This is based on analyzing displacement histograms of traces crossing boundaries.

claim: Rad52 molecules adopt the diffusive behavior of the surrounding Rad52 molecules in their environment.
source: In other words, Rad52 molecules clearly change diffusion coefficient when entering or escaping repair foci, adopting the diffusive behavior of the surrounding Rad52 molecules in their environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sharp change in diffusion at boundaries.

claim: Both foci induced by 1 DSB and 2 DSBs exhibit similar mobility.
source: Using strains expressing Rad52-mMaple with high photo-activation, we found that both foci exhibit similar mobility (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on comparing displacement histograms of whole foci.

claim: Foci induced by 2 DSBs are larger than those induced by a single DSB (170 ± 20 nm versus 116 ± 20 nm respectively).
source: We found that foci induced by 2 DSBs are larger than those induced by a single DSB, (170 ± 20 nm versus 116 ± 20 nm respectively, p=1×10−4, Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from live PALM with statistical significance.

claim: The number of Rad52 molecules forming foci varies from 880 ± 600 for 1 DSB induced foci to 2300 ± 811 for 2-DSBs foci.
source: In addition, the number of Rad52 molecules forming foci varies from 880 ± 600 for 1 DSB induced foci to 2300 ± 811 for 2-DSBs foci (p=8×10−4, Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from live PALM with statistical significance.

claim: Focus density is indistinguishable between foci induced by 1 versus 2 DSBs.
source: Thus, focus density is indistinguishable between foci induced by 1 versus 2 DSBs (Figure 6C, right panel, p=0.73, Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: This is based on comparing density measurements with statistical testing.

claim: Upon 1 DSB, Rad52 diffuses inside foci with a confinement radius of 124 ± 3 nm.
source: Here, we found that upon 1 DSB, Rad52 diffuse inside foci with smaller confinement radius (124 ± 3 nm) compared to foci induced by 2 DSBs (156 ± 3 nm), supporting the second view where foci fuse (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a measurement from MSD analysis.

claim: Upon 2 DSBs, Rad52 diffuses inside foci with a confinement radius of 156 ± 3 nm.
source: Here, we found that upon 1 DSB, Rad52 diffuse inside foci with smaller confinement radius (124 ± 3 nm) compared to foci induced by 2 DSBs (156 ± 3 nm), supporting the second view where foci fuse (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a measurement from MSD analysis.

claim: The confinement radius found by SPT is very close to the mean size of Rad52 foci obtained by live PALM.
source: Importantly, this confinement radius found by SPT is very close to the mean size of Rad52 foci previously obtained by live PALM.
evidence: This is a comparison between two different measurement methods.

claim: The correlation between focus size and confinement radius indicates that Rad52 is able to explore the entire focus space.
source: The correlation between focus size and confinement radius indicates that Rad52 is able to explore the entire focus space.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation between two measurements.

claim: There is a region of attraction for Rad52 molecules inside the focus with an average movement towards the center.
source: Concentrating on molecules close to the boundary, we identified a region of attraction with an average movement of molecules towards the center of the focus (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on analyzing radial displacement of molecules.

claim: In response to a DSB, Rad52 diffusion is not altered in the nucleus outside of foci.
source: In response to a DSB, Rad52 diffusion is not altered in the nucleus, thus Rad52 molecules likely do not exhibit a strong collective or directive motion toward the damaged DNA site.
evidence: This is based on comparing diffusion outside foci before and after DSB induction.

claim: Rad52 molecules likely do not exhibit a strong collective or directive motion toward the damaged DNA site.
source: In response to a DSB, Rad52 diffusion is not altered in the nucleus, thus Rad52 molecules likely do not exhibit a strong collective or directive motion toward the damaged DNA site.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of change in diffusion outside foci.

claim: Rad52 molecules arrive at the DSB by simple diffusion.
source: They rather arrive by simple diffusion at the DSB where they bind ssDNA coated by the RPA complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of directed motion.

claim: The focus is formed by a small seed of Rad52 molecules bound to RPA coated ssDNA, around which a large cloud of Rad52 rapidly diffuses.
source: The focus is then formed by a small seed of Rad52 molecules bound to RPA coated ssDNA, around which a large cloud of Rad52 rapidly diffuse exploring the whole focus.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the mobility and confinement data.

claim: Rad52 foci are dense but surprisingly dynamic.
source: Similar to LLPS, Rad52 foci are dense but surprisingly dynamic: Rad52 molecules inside foci are ~6 times more mobile than ssDNA-binding proteins Rfa1 and exhibit permanent exchange with the rest of the nucleus.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Rad52 molecules inside foci are approximately 6 times more mobile than ssDNA-binding proteins Rfa1.
source: Similar to LLPS, Rad52 foci are dense but surprisingly dynamic: Rad52 molecules inside foci are ~6 times more mobile than ssDNA-binding proteins Rfa1 and exhibit permanent exchange with the rest of the nucleus.
evidence: This is based on comparing diffusion coefficients.

claim: Rad52 molecules are retained inside the focus by a potential.
source: Rad52 molecules are retained inside the focus by a potential.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of radial motion showing attraction toward the center.

claim: The existence of an attractive potential supports a model where DNA is dispensable to maintain the phase separation once a given saturating concentration of multivalent binder molecules is reached.
source: The existence of such attractive potential supports a model where DNA is dispensable to maintain the phase separation once a given saturating concentration of multivalent binder molecules is reached.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the attractive potential finding.

claim: Rad52 foci exhibit many features of LLPS at the microscopic level.
source: Overall, our results at the single molecule level reveal that Rad52 foci exhibit many features of LLPS at the microscopic level, consistent with recent studies using macroscopic criteria both in yeast and in human cells (Altmeyer et al., 2015; Kilic et al., 2019; Oshidari et al., 2020; Pessina et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence with citations to supporting studies.

claim: Assuming Brownian diffusion, a diffusion coefficient of 1.15 μm2/s implies that Rad52 can go across a yeast nucleus in as little as 700 ms.
source: Assuming Brownian diffusion, a diffusion coefficient of 1.15 μm2/s implies that Rad52 can go across a yeast nucleus in as little as 700 ms.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured diffusion coefficient.

claim: The dynamic viscosity inside yeast nuclei is approximately 100 times higher than water at 20°C.
source: Moreover, tracking free Halo-NLS, we estimate the dynamic viscosity inside yeast nuclei to 0.1 Pa.s, compared to 10−3 Pa.s for water at 20°C, 0.013 P.s in Hela cells nuclei (Liang et al., 2009) and 6 Pa.s for honey.
evidence: This is calculated by comparing the measured viscosity (0.1 Pa.s) to water (10^-3 Pa.s).

claim: The viscosity inside repair foci is 8 to 20 times higher than the nucleus viscosity estimated before damage.
source: These viscosities are respectively 8 to 20 times higher than the nucleus viscosity estimated before damage (νyeast nucleus = 0.122 ± 0.004 Pa.s).
evidence: This is calculated by comparing viscosities inside and outside foci.

claim: The viscosity inside repair foci appears similar in yeast and humans (approximately 1-2.5 Pa.s).
source: In human cells (U2OS), a similar viscosity inside repair foci has been found (2.5 Pa.s) by measuring the diffusion of 53BP1 molecules within foci (Pessina et al., 2019). Although human nuclei are ~25 times less viscous than yeast, the viscosity inside repair foci appears similar in yeast and humans.
evidence: This is a comparison with a cited study in human cells.

claim: Most of Rad52 molecules are not bound to the Rfa1-coated ssDNA inside foci.
source: Such differences in diffusion coefficient and type of motion between Rad52 and Rfa1 indicate that most of Rad52 molecules are not bound to the Rfa1-coated ssDNA inside foci, in agreement with (Essers et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing Rad52 and Rfa1 mobility with a citation for support.

claim: The rapid exchange rate observed for individual Rad52 molecules is in good agreement with FLIP experiments in yeast cells.
source: The rapid exchange rate observed here for individual Rad52 molecules is in good agreement with FLIP (fluorescence loss in photobleaching) experiments in yeast cells (Oshidari et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison with a cited study using a different technique.

claim: FRAP experiments in mammalian cells revealed that Rad54 and Rad52 inside foci rapidly exchange with the rest of the nucleus while Rad51 stays immobilized at the site of DNA damage.
source: Fluorescence Recovery After Photobleaching (FRAP) experiments in mammalian cells also revealed different exchange rates and residence times depending on the repair proteins: Rad54 and Rad52 inside foci rapidly exchange with the rest of the nucleus while Rad51 stays immobilized at the site of DNA damage (Essers et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a study in mammalian cells.

claim: If Rad52 were rapidly binding and unbinding to ssDNA, the binding dissociation constant would have to be very weak (Kd >> 2 μM) to be consistent with the smooth displacement histogram.
source: To be consistent with the smoothness of our displacement histogram, the binding specificity would have to be very weak, Kd = 1/(4 D a τ) ≫ 2 μM (Berg and Purcell, 1977), where a ≈ 10 nm is the linear size of the binding site, D ≈ 1 μm2/s, and τ is the mean bound time ≪ 20 ms, conservatively assuming diffusion-limited binding.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the lack of multi-modal distribution in the data.

claim: The calculated dissociation constant (Kd >> 2 μM) is 20 to 400 times larger than the values observed in vitro.
source: This dissociation constant is 20 to 400 times larger than the values observed in vitro (Saotome et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison with in vitro measurements from a cited study.

claim: Only a very small fraction of Rad52 molecules are bound to the Rfa1-coated ssDNA.
source: Altogether, our data and analysis rather suggest that most Rad52 freely diffuse inside foci and only a very small fraction of Rad52 molecules are bound to the Rfa1-coated ssDNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of binding kinetics and displacement distributions.

claim: With single molecule experiments, it is very unlikely to catch the few bound Rad52 molecules.
source: Since with single molecule experiments, we can follow only a fraction of the molecules, it is very unlikely to catch the few bound molecules in our assay.
evidence: This is a limitation of the experimental approach stated by the authors.

claim: In the LLPS model, proteins self-organize into liquid-like droplets that grow around a nucleation site.
source: A third scenario is the Liquid-Liquid Phase Separation (LLPS) Model, also referred to as 'Droplet Model' (Hyman et al., 2014). Unlike the binding and the PPPS models, in LLPS, proteins self-organize into liquid-like droplets that grow around a nucleation site allowing certain molecules to become concentrated while excluding others.
evidence: This is a description of the LLPS model with a citation.

claim: In LLPS, one should distinguish scaffold proteins (able to initiate phase separation) from client proteins (concentrating within the droplet without being responsible for its formation).
source: In this framework, one should distinguish proteins able to initiate a liquid phase separation on their own (scaffold proteins) from proteins concentrating and diffusing freely within this droplet without being responsible for its formation (client proteins) (Banani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conceptual distinction in LLPS models with a citation.

claim: Rad52 might not be the main driving molecule responsible for the LLPS formed at the damaged site.
source: Here, we found that upon different levels of Rad52 over-expression, the background concentration increases as predicted for a 'client' (see Appendix 1 and Appendix 1- figure 1) suggesting that Rad52 might not be the main driving molecule responsible for the LLPS formed at the damaged site.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on over-expression experiments.

claim: Several DSBs coalesce and dissociate independently of Rad52.
source: This is in agreement with the observation that several DSBs coalesce and dissociate independently of Rad52 (Waterman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the conclusion about Rad52 not being the main driver.

claim: LLPS composed by multiple proteins with heterotypic multicomponent interactions do not exhibit a fixed saturation concentration.
source: However, a recent study pointed out that LLPS composed by multiple proteins with heterotypic multicomponent interactions do not exhibit a fixed saturation concentration (Riback et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a recent study.

claim: In human cells, DSB-induced transcriptional promoters drive RNA synthesis and stimulate phase separation of repair proteins.
source: In human cells, it has been suggested that DSB-induced transcriptional promoters drive RNA synthesis and stimulate phase separation of repair proteins (Pessina et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a study in human cells.

claim: Sub-nuclear compartments can phase separate by PPPS and collapse of such foci is sometimes wrongly interpreted as a fusion of liquid droplets.
source: For example, sub-nuclear compartments can phase separate by PPPS and collapse of such foci is sometimes wrongly interpreted as a fusion of liquid droplets (Erdel et al., 2020; McSwiggen et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is stated with citations as a caution about interpreting experimental observations.

claim: When all Rad52 molecules are SUMOylated, Rad52 foci transition to a gel-like sub-compartment.
source: We propose that when all Rad52 molecules are SUMOylated, Rad52 foci transition to a gel-like sub-compartment where most of the molecules are still free to explore the whole focus but much slower than in wild type cells.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the SUMOylation data.

claim: The formation of LLPS around damage sites may be a mechanism to increase the pool of molecules at the DSB.
source: Since SUMOylated Rad52 foci are smaller, it is possible that the formation of LLPS around damage sites is a mechanism to increase the pull of molecules at the DSB.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the SUMOylation results.

claim: The high internal dynamics of Rad52 inside foci and the capacity of Rad52 to explore the whole focus are conserved in diploid cells where DNA damage can be repaired.
source: We thus conclude that the high internal dynamics of Rad52 inside foci, and the capacity of Rad52 to explore the whole focus conserved in diploid cells where DNA damage can be repaired.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing haploid and diploid cell data.
